lead: A proposition is a declarative statement that is definitely true or definitely false. Propositional logic gives it symbols and connectives, so a sentence can be turned into a formula whose truth table shows every possible case. Truth tables expose tautologies, formulas that are true in every row, and they are the base for proof rules, digital circuits, program conditions and database filters. This chapter sets up the connectives, the table method and the three classifications you will use in later chapters on equivalence, normal forms and inference.

blocks.text: A proposition is a declarative statement that has exactly one truth value: T (true) or F (false). '7 is prime' is a proposition with value T. '2+2=5' is a proposition with value F. 'Close the door' is a command, 'Is it raining?' is a question, and 'x+3=10' has no fixed value until x is chosen. These are not propositions in this chapter. A propositional variable such as p, q or r stands for a proposition. A compound proposition is built from variables and connectives.

items: Negation ¬p is 'not p'; it is T when p is F, and F when p is T.
Conjunction p∧q is 'p and q'; it is T only when both p and q are T.
Disjunction p∨q is 'p or q' in the inclusive sense; it is T when at least one of p, q is T.
Exclusive or p⊕q is T when exactly one of p, q is T; some syllabi call it XOR.
Implication p→q is 'if p then q'; it is F only in the row p=T, q=F. p is the antecedent and q is the consequent.
Biconditional p↔q is 'p if and only if q'; it is T when p and q have the same truth value; some syllabi call it equivalence.

blocks.text: The connectives turn small statements into larger formulas. The figure's formula, (p→q)∨(q→p), says 'either p implies q, or q implies p'. Its table is built in the example.

A truth table lists every assignment of T and F to the variables and shows the value of each subformula. With n variables there are 2<sup>n</sup> rows. Two variables use 4 rows; three variables use 8 rows.

items: Write the variables in a fixed order, then add one column for each connective, working from the innermost brackets outward.
Fill the variable columns with all 2<sup>n</sup> assignments. For two variables a reliable order is TT, TF, FT, FF.
Evaluate negation first, then conjunction, then disjunction or exclusive or, then implication, then biconditional. Brackets override this order.
Read the final column. If every entry is T, the formula is a tautology. If every entry is F, it is a contradiction. If it has both T and F, it is a contingency.

blocks.text: For example, p∨¬p is a tautology: if p is T the left part is T, and if p is F the negation is T. p∧¬p is a contradiction: no assignment makes both p and not p true. p→q is a contingency: it is T in three rows and F in the row p=T, q=F. The figure's formula is a tautology because its final column has T in all four rows. Logical equivalences are proved with such tables; see 1.2. Normal forms record the rows that matter; see 1.3.

Precedence fixes the order when brackets are missing. From tightest to loosest: ¬, then ∧, then ∨ and ⊕, then →, then ↔. So ¬p∨q∧r→s is read as ((¬p)∨(q∧r))→s. When in doubt, add brackets; the examiner marks the table, not your memory of precedence.

blocks.where: p, q, r and s are propositions; ¬ is negation, ∧ is and, ∨ is or, and → is implication. Brackets show the grouping forced by precedence.

blocks.text: Boolean values also appear as bits inside integers. In C, C++, Java and Python, & is bitwise AND, | is bitwise OR, and ^ is bitwise XOR. Take 6 and 3. In binary, 6 = 110₂ and 3 = 011₂. Bit by bit: 6 & 3 = 010₂ = 2; 6 | 3 = 111₂ = 7; 6 ^ 3 = 101₂ = 5. Each bit position behaves like one row of a truth table, but the whole integer is not a proposition. The same connectives drive logic gates and program conditions.
Propositional formulas become arguments when you attach premises and a conclusion. The validity rules are in 1.4. Quantifiers, which let a formula speak about all or some objects, are in 1.6.

figure.caption: The table for (p→q)∨(q→p): columns are p, q, p→q, q→p, and the final OR. The final column is T in every row, so the formula is a tautology.

spec.title: (p→q)∨(q→p)
spec.aria: A four-row truth table for (p→q)∨(q→p); the last column is true in every row.

examples.question: Construct the truth table for (p→q)∨(q→p). Classify the formula as a tautology, contradiction or contingency.
steps: Two variables p and q give 2² = 4 rows: (T,T), (T,F), (F,T), (F,F).
Compute p→q. It is F only for (T,F); the column is T, F, T, T.
Compute q→p. It is F only for (F,T); the column is T, T, F, T.
OR the two columns row by row: T∨T=T; F∨T=T; T∨F=T; T∨T=T. Final column: T, T, T, T, encoded as 1, 1, 1, 1.
Every row is T, so no assignment makes the formula false.
examples.answer: The formula (p→q)∨(q→p) is a tautology; its final column is T in all four rows, encoded as 1, 1, 1, 1.
examples.check:
rows = [(True, True), (True, False), (False, True), (False, False)]
for p, q in rows:
    p_imp_q = (not p) or q
    q_imp_p = (not q) or p
    final = p_imp_q or q_imp_p
    print(int(final))

traps: p→q is false only when p is T and q is F. A common error is to mark it false when p is F; then the implication is T by definition. Also p→q is not q→p.
The English word 'or' can be inclusive or exclusive. In p∨q, assume inclusive unless the question says XOR (⊕).
¬ binds tighter than ∧, and ∧ tighter than ∨. Without brackets, ¬p∨q means (¬p)∨q, not ¬(p∨q).
A tautology needs T in every row, not T in the rows you checked. With three variables there are 8 rows; missing rows is the usual lost mark.
p↔q is true when both are T or both are F. Do not confuse it with p→q, which is true in three of the four rows.

quiz.q: Define a proposition and give one example with its truth value.
quiz.a: A declarative statement with exactly one truth value T or F. '7 is prime' has value T.

quiz.q: For p=T and q=F, write the truth values of p∧q and p∨q.
Why is 'x+3=10' not a proposition in this chapter?
quiz.a: x is not fixed; the statement has no single truth value until x is chosen.

quiz.q: Explain why p→q is true when p=F and q=F.
quiz.a: Implication is false only in row p=T, q=F; all other rows are T. It does not claim p caused q.

quiz.q: Construct the final column of (p→q)∧(q→p) for rows TT, TF, FT, FF.
quiz.a: TT: T∧T=T; TF: F∧T=F; FT: T∧F=F; FF: T∧T=T. Final column T, F, F, T.

quiz.q: A formula has final column T, F, T, F for four rows. Is it a tautology, contradiction or contingency? Justify.
quiz.a: Contingency: it has both T and F in its final column, so some assignments make it true and some make it false.

beyond: Not for the exam. Propositional logic is the input language of SAT solvers, programs that check millions of clauses for hardware and software verification. The same truth tables appear in logic-gate design, where AND, OR and XOR gates are built from transistors. Database engines simplify WHERE conditions using Boolean algebra, and SMT solvers add arithmetic to propositional reasoning. Search for 'SAT solver', 'SMT' and 'Boolean satisfiability' to go further.
